trials.notes: Passed 6/6 frozen cases. All API methods used are documented. Main penalty: it used WP_HTML_Processor, and even tried create_full_parser() before create_fragment(), for a flat source-order class edit where the docs recommend WP_HTML_Tag_Processor. It did use bookmarks and get_updated_html() correctly, but next_token() was more complex than needed and it never checked get_last_error() or paused_at_incomplete_token() before trusting an end-to-end scan for the last H2.

Passed 6/6 frozen cases. All API methods used are documented. The traversal is cleaner than trial-1: next_tag(), repeated bookmark, seek(), add_class(), release_bookmark(), and get_updated_html(). The main issue is processor choice: WP_HTML_Processor is unnecessary and less robust for a flat tag/class edit. Its get_last_error()/paused_at_incomplete_token() guard is documented and cautious, but it can over-reject inputs that the Tag Processor could still edit byte-preservingly.

Passed 6/6 frozen cases. This closely matches the documented and canonical pattern: construct WP_HTML_Tag_Processor directly, scan H2 tags with next_tag(), keep one literal bookmark updated to the latest match, seek back, add_class(), release the bookmark, and return get_updated_html(). Minor deductions only for not checking set_bookmark()/seek failure beyond the final seek branch and not making an explicit incomplete-input policy.

failure_analysis:
All trials passed every frozen case, so there are no failed hidden cases to attribute. The docs worked well for this task in several places: the Tag Processor overview explicitly says to use it for flat, position-based tag/class edits; next_tag() documents string and array tag-name queries; add_class() documents creating/appending the class while preserving existing classes; get_updated_html() is clearly presented as the correct output API for queued edits; and the Tag Processor set_bookmark() section directly explains the general pattern of re-setting one bookmark on each match and seeking to it after the scan.

The near-misses were concentrated around processor selection. Trials 1 and 2 both chose WP_HTML_Processor despite explaining a flat tag edit. That choice passed the simple cases but inherits HTML Processor abort behavior on unsupported markup, which can make a 'last matching tag' scan incomplete. Trial 1 in particular did not check get_last_error() after a whole-input scan; on unsupported markup after an earlier H2 it could treat the last successfully visited H2 as the global last H2. Trial 2 did check parser error and incomplete-token state, which follows the HTML Processor safety guidance, but that same choice means it may return the original HTML in cases where the Tag Processor could safely mark the last source-order H2. These are not frozen-test failures, but they show that the docs still leave room for models to overuse the tree-aware processor for byte-preserving flat edits.

doc_gaps.location: WP_HTML_Processor overview / Which processor should I use?
doc_gaps.problem: The docs say the lighter Tag Processor suffices for flat attribute and class edits, but two subjects still selected the HTML Processor for a source-order 'last matching tag' edit.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short decision note: if the match is based only on source-order tag name, class, or attributes, prefer WP_HTML_Tag_Processor plus next_tag(); reserve WP_HTML_Processor for matches depending on DOM structure, subtree boundaries, implied tags, text extraction, or normalization.

doc_gaps.problem: The Tag Processor docs clearly mention re-setting one bookmark to remember the last match, but the HTML Processor's rendered set_bookmark() section is less explicit about re-setting an existing bookmark name moving it.
doc_gaps.suggestion: State in both rendered method docs that calling set_bookmark() again with the same literal name moves that bookmark to the current token, which is the intended bounded-memory pattern for remembering the latest match in a scan.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs warn that unsupported markup aborts the HTML Processor, but they do not make the consequence vivid for scans whose answer depends on reaching the end, such as last-match, count-all, or collect-all operations.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add guidance that any HTML Processor scan whose result depends on seeing the entire remaining input must treat non-null get_last_error() as an incomplete result before seeking back or mutating based on what was found so far.

doc_gaps.problem: For functions accepting either complete documents or fragments, subjects guessed factory order instead of recognizing that a flat byte-preserving edit avoids the factory choice entirely.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add factory-choice guidance saying that document-vs-fragment ambiguity is a reason to use WP_HTML_Tag_Processor when tree semantics are not required; when tree semantics are required, callers should choose the factory from their input contract rather than silently trying both as a default pattern.

doc_gaps.problem: The incomplete-token docs explain how scanning pauses, but do not clearly state the policy implications for earlier complete matches and queued edits. This can lead either to ignoring truncation when completeness matters or over-rejecting when the requested edit only touches an earlier complete token.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Clarify that earlier complete tokens and bookmarks remain editable after a pause, and advise callers to choose explicitly between best-effort byte-preserving updates and returning the original input when their result requires a complete scan.
